cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman sentenced to 3 years in prison for running illegal med spa out of backyard shed
cards.body:
Rosa Mena, 50, has been sentenced to three years in prison and five years of probation after operating an unlicensed medical spa out of a shed in her Port St. Lucie backyard. Mena ran the business, called Miracle Hand and Spa, at her residence in the 5000 block of Northwest Coosa Drive.

The case came to light in May 2025 when a victim reported partial facial paralysis after receiving 62 units of Botox injections from Mena. The victim, who had been referred by coworkers, paid $325 for the service. When confronted, Mena initially refunded the money and asked the victim to return for another injection of vitamins to reverse the effects. The victim later requested to see Mena's medical license and discovered an altered phlebotomy certificate that had expired in February 2024. Mena told the victim she was a doctor from the Dominican Republic.

A multi-agency investigation involving Port St. Lucie Police, PSL Code Enforcement, the PSL Building Department, the PSL Business Tax office, and the Florida Department of Health led to a search warrant. Detectives found medical beds, fat sculpting machines, laser hair removal equipment, laser liposuction machines, and injection devices for fillers and Botox. Mena was charged with three counts of aggravated battery causing bodily harm, three counts of practicing medicine without an active license, fraud charges, and use of a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island officials confident despite state report warning of 9 feet of flooding at emergency center
cards.body:
Jupiter Island leaders say they are prepared for future storms despite a new state vulnerability assessment warning that 103 critical town assets face flooding risk, including the town's Emergency Operations Center, which could see up to 9 feet of floodwater.

The Florida Department of Environmental Protection report identified 68 stormwater facilities, 17 historic sites, conservation lands, and key evacuation routes at risk. Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field told investigators the findings confirm what town leaders already knew. "The town's been working for a long time on an assessment of our erosion issues, our vulnerability issues," Field said. Beach District Director John Duchok said the assessment will create a roadmap to prioritize improvements.

The report comes after a separate state study warned severe erosion could one day split the island. Field said the goal is to document risks and compete for state and federal funding to address vulnerabilities. "We absolutely intend to do that. There's a window that opened up June 1 for applications for funding for this year, and we will certainly take advantage of that," Field said. He added that evacuation orders would be issued well before floodwaters threaten roadways and that the town has a backup facility on the mainland to maintain operations during emergencies.

cards.headline: Florida lawmakers pass $200,000 property tax exemption increase pending November vote
cards.teaser: Florida lawmakers approved a measure to raise the homestead exemption from $50,000 to $250,000, but voters must approve it in November.
cards.body:
Florida lawmakers passed a property tax cut proposal Tuesday that would increase the homestead exemption from $50,000 to $250,000 over two years, with inflation adjustments beginning in 2029. The measure requires approval from 60% of voters in November. The bill would also lower assessment caps on non-homesteaded properties from 10% to 5%.

Experts remain divided on potential consequences. Real estate attorney Steve Wallace raised the possibility of new non-ad valorem taxes or increased fees. CPA Paul Miller suggested businesses could carry more financial burden through fees. Municipal attorney Raul Gastesi predicted home prices could increase. All four experts acknowledged significant unknowns about how counties and municipalities might respond to decreasing property tax revenue.

cards.headline: 12 children from Make-A-Wish Foundation sworn in as junior deputies by St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office
cards.teaser: Sheriff Richard Del Toro swore in 12 young heroes as junior deputies on Wednesday, including twins Mia and Daryl Nyack, whose bone marrow donation saved his sister's life.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office swore in 12 children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation as junior deputies on Wednesday. Sheriff Richard Del Toro presided over the ceremony, calling it "one of the greatest days in my career." The junior deputies received badges, toured the sheriff's office, and witnessed demonstrations from the SWAT team, K-9 unit, and helicopter.

Among the honorees were twins Mia and Daryl Nyack. In 2023, Mia was diagnosed with aplastic anemia and needed a bone marrow transplant. Daryl donated his bone marrow to save his sister's life. Another junior deputy, Tobias, was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia in 2022 and has since recovered. Their parents expressed gratitude to the Sheriff's Office for celebrating their children as community heroes.

Town leaders requested the assessment to help document risks and create a roadmap for improvements. The Broadway hit "Beetlejuice" runs through June 7 at the Kravis Center's Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall in West Palm Beach. Actor Ryan Stajmiger plays the mischievous demon in the striped suit, bringing the character from Tim Burton's 1988 film to life on stage. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a "strange and unusual" teen whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and the trouble-making demon.

Stajmiger highlights the fun of breaking the fourth wall and interacting directly with audiences. He shared a memorable early performance moment when a wig change mishap left him bald on stage. Show times include 7:30 p.m. on June 3 and 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50 at kravis.org.

cards.headline: Paddlers will cross 80 miles of Atlantic Ocean to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 for cystic fibrosis
cards.teaser: More than 100 endurance paddlers will launch from Bimini at midnight and arrive after 12 to 16 hours of paddling.
cards.body:
More than 100 paddlers will launch from Bimini, Bahamas at midnight on June 13 for the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis, traveling 80 miles across the open Atlantic Ocean to Lake Worth Beach. The 12 to 16-hour endurance trek benefits the Piper's Angels Foundation, established by event founder Travis Suit in honor of his daughter Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4.

All paddlers must wear U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation devices, waterproof whistles, reflective gear, and GPS trackers. Participants are required to raise at least $2,000, with crew or virtual participants having a $500 minimum. The four-day event begins June 10 with activities including a beach cleanup, Paddle Out Rose Ceremony, and safety briefings. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 to celebrate paddlers' arrival.

hero.headline: St. Petersburg votes to evaluate leaving Duke Energy Florida for municipal utility
hero.body:
The St. Petersburg City Council voted to evaluate whether the city should leave Duke Energy Florida and form its own electric utility. The tight vote marked a major step toward the city seriously considering municipal power generation and distribution.

The decision comes amid ongoing concerns about electric rates and service in the Tampa Bay region. If St. Petersburg ultimately decides to establish its own utility, it would join a handful of Florida municipalities that operate independent electric systems rather than relying on investor-owned companies like Duke Energy Florida.

The evaluation process will examine the financial feasibility, infrastructure requirements, and potential customer savings of forming a municipal utility. City officials will need to analyze the costs of purchasing or building necessary infrastructure, staffing requirements, and the legal process for separating from Duke Energy Florida's service territory.

The vote represents the beginning of what could be a lengthy process. Municipal utilities in Florida operate in cities including Jacksonville, Orlando, Tallahassee, and Gainesville, where local governments maintain direct control over electric generation and distribution. Supporters of municipal power often cite greater local control and potential cost savings, while critics point to the significant upfront costs and complexity of establishing new utility operations.

hero.headline: Jupiter Island faces risk of 9-foot flooding at emergency center, state report warns
hero.body:
Jupiter Island's Emergency Operations Center could see up to 9 feet of floodwater during future storms, according to a new vulnerability assessment by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. The report identified 103 critical town assets at risk of flooding, including 68 stormwater facilities, 17 historic sites, conservation lands, and key evacuation routes.

Town leaders say the findings confirm what they already knew when they requested the assessment. "I would say not," Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said when asked if he was surprised by the report. "The town's been working for a long time on an assessment of our erosion issues, our vulnerability issues." Field said the town feels prepared because evacuation orders would be issued well before floodwaters threaten roadways, and the town maintains a backup facility on the mainland.

The findings follow a separate state study warning that severe erosion could one day break through part of the island. Field said the town's goal is to document the risks and compete for state and federal funding to address vulnerabilities. "There's a window that opened up June 1 for applications for funding for this year, and we will certainly take advantage of that," Field said. The 126-page report also warns that stormwater systems face some of the greatest risks, noting they can fail during the very flooding events they are designed to manage. Beach District Director John Duchok said the vulnerability assessment will create a roadmap for addressing the highest priorities first.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman sentenced to 3 years in prison for running illegal med spa out of backyard shed
cards.body:
Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St. Lucie has been sentenced to three years in prison and five years of probation after operating an illegal medical spa out of a shed in her backyard. The business, called Miracle Hand and Spa, came to the attention of authorities in May 2025 when a victim reported partial facial paralysis after receiving 62 units of Botox injections from Mena at the makeshift facility.

The victim, who had been referred to Mena by coworkers, paid $325 for the services. When she reported the paralysis, Mena refunded the money but asked the victim to return for another injection of vitamins to reverse the problem. After the paralysis persisted, the victim asked to see Mena's medical license. Mena provided an altered certificate of phlebotomy that had expired in February 2024. Mena also claimed to be a doctor from the Dominican Republic in an attempt to reassure the victim.

A multi-agency investigation by Port St. Lucie Police, PSL Code Enforcement, the PSL Building Department, PSL Business Tax, and the Florida Department of Health led to a search warrant at Mena's residence in the 5000 block of Northwest Coosa Drive. Detectives found medical beds, fat sculpting machines, laser hair removal equipment, laser liposuction machines, and injection devices for fillers and Botox. Mena was convicted on nine charges including three counts of aggravated battery causing bodily harm, three counts of practicing medicine without an active license, fraud charges, and use of a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony.

cards.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway as revitalization project begins in Vero Beach
cards.teaser: Crews began tearing down portions of the Indian River Mall this week, marking the start of a major revitalization project for the long-struggling shopping cente.
cards.body:
Crews began tearing down portions of the Indian River Mall this week, marking the start of a major revitalization project for the long-struggling shopping center. Joseph Scarfone, the project manager working on the redevelopment, said crews are working on the first phase by taking down the Macy's and the former Sears location.

Neighbors gathered in the parking lot to watch the demolition of the mall, which many said had declined significantly over the years. Mary Alice Stopyra said she was happy to see the structure come down because it had degraded over time. Mark Manera from Vero Beach, who had visited the mall for years, described it as looking like a graveyard and said he saw a steady decline year after year.

Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a new indoor and outdoor shopping center featuring around 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants and possible residential spaces. He described the project as a city within a city and said residents would no longer see the dead mall that had been collecting cobwebs for the last 12 years. The project manager said he hopes the first phase can be completed by 2027, while crews continue working on permitting for the rest of the development.
